en: I bow to that glorious Lord, the playful Time who dwells in speech;
he who, as Rāma, the delighter of the beautiful women, performed his divine sports while residing in Ayodhyā. || 1 ||

I bow to that divine Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is to be served and studied in reverse order, who is beloved by Rādhā, who is worshipped by the gopīs, who is the delight of the gopīs, who is the ornament of the forehead of Lakṣmī, and who is the supreme savior. || 1 ||
That city named Sāketa was preeminent, radiant with Brahmins, a support for the noble,
ancient, victorious over the gods, foremost in trustworthiness, and resounding with the cries of birds.
In reverse order,
she is the foremost abode in the ocean of vowels, accompanied by horses;
she is the city of ignorance, the conqueror of old age, the one attained by Rādhā, the radiant limit of knowledge, the sacrificial offering, and she whose hair is like the sky.
The earth was a new pond for the multitude of palaces possessing the splendor of solid essence, a burden of desire;
it was a land where the beautiful trees possessed forms as red as the cries of cranes and were thick with the sound of cranes.
This [city] has many temples of the gods, is thick with the essence of thrones,
possesses faultless palaces, and has guards stationed at its mango groves. || 3 ||
May the obstruction of sin be equal to the abode of Rāma;
may she who does not know the essence of the great imperishable syllable (Oṃ) have no luster.
The high-minded descendant of Yadu protected the earth in reverse order;
those gods of unblemished luster honored her who possessed equal virtues.
That which is profound, yogic, passionate, pertaining to the sacrificial fire, gentle, and blissful— known as cool and expansive— is protected by the destroyer of the fearsome ones.
He is the reverse of that, the protector, the one who has abandoned fear, the illustrious, the fearless, the expanded, the cool, the renowned;
he is the leader in happiness, gentle, the one who leads, indeed the singer of songs, the one who is sung about by warriors.
O you who possess a delicate luster like that of the moon, who have taken recourse to the dance of the arising of aesthetic flavor,
and who are equal to the autumnal moon with its petals of blossoming lotuses, you are most deeply bowed in devotion.
By him, the reverse was bestowed; from Gopāla came Amarāvikā,
and from him, who was the essence of the king’s daughter, came Ramā, the flower of Rāmā, who took refuge in him.

May the one named Rāma—who is ever free from weariness, compassionate, and possessed of unassailable splendor; who purifies his enemies; who is the self-luminous essence of the bliss of the primordial letter *Ka*; and who is the source of the body of Gaurī, the daughter of Bhūri—the Lord of Mountains—be my refuge. (7)
By that Pārijāta tree, which was contrary [to the usual order],
which was like Meru, the earth, the quarters, the sky, the atoms, and the flowers, and which brought joy through its laughter-like brilliance,
the Yadavas were refreshed as if by nectar; it was new, free from fatigue, and equal to the gods.
In those abodes, together with Sītā, whose eyes were dark like the *sārasa* crane, he sported fearlessly, destroying the essence of the demons who were full of terror.
In reverse order:
*vilomaṃ hārasārasumāramyakṣemerehavisādhvasā yātasīsumadhāmnābhūkṣitādhāmasasārasā*. (This verse, when read backward, yields the same sequence of syllables.)
She shone with a mass of sins,
possessed by fury, having gone into the midst of the assembly, and having attained her essence while being tormented.
In this [verse], due to the perception of essential meaning in reverse order, there is heat accompanied by distress; therein,
through the power of another, the illustrious one, possessed of impetuosity and sin, has gone.
Alas, Kaikeyī, who brought great torment, has now become a source of great joy; she who was once a burden of unbearable weight has become a single, incomparable refuge.
In reverse order,
she whose abode is established in each of the syllables *ha-ha-dā-ha-ma-yī-ke*, who possesses a face with a constant smile, who is radiant like the sun, and who is bowed down by the path of anger.
Ah! This one, who goes toward Rāvaṇa with a radiant, steady, and firm intellect, is superior to [Rāma], who was led away by his father’s respect for the boon, honor, truth, shame, and affection. 11.
The reverse order [of the letters] is: Saumya-gāna-varārohā-parodhī-ra-sthira-svabhā-hodarāt-trāpita-hrī-satya-asadana-māravā. (11)
She who was born from the daughter of Yāna-yānaghada, the offspring of Rasā, went to the son of Ahi-viyāta;
she was modest, virtuous, and free from the affliction of sorrow.
By her, whose intellect was dense with sorrow, who was ashamed by the fall of the sun-like king, and who had committed no offense, he caused the pain of separation to be experienced in reverse.
Alas! By the greatness of the fire of his wrath, born from pride in his lineage and asceticism, he has fallen into a state of utter ruin, having reached Bharadvāja who was difficult to approach.
"O you who have come from afar with a voice that bears the burden of words as noble as a great piece of wood, why do you approach our gate in this contrary manner? (13)

With a journey that was lofty yet free from calamity, he reached the mountain peak— the abode of the Sugata— which bore the splendor of a mass of lightning, emitted the fragrance of the wind, and was the station of the Sage.
The reverse journey results in the exhaustion of the fruits of one's sins; it is the supreme destroyer of great transgressions.
It is as fragrant as the *gandharva* tree and as beautiful as the courtyard of *raṃbhā*.
Then King Pradama, having destroyed the Daṇḍakas and removed all afflictions, became a destroyer of disease;
he was possessed of equal conduct and was not to be enjoyed by others, nor did he occupy their seat.
He was not one who led away those who were not his eternal objects of enjoyment;
he was the bestower of the fragrance of the pleasure of Ahalyā’s husband, which removes the pride of Hārikā.
He who knows the secret of subduing Māra, whose throat is like a water-pot,
who is the destroyer of the various defects of the serpents, and who is the essence of the tree-bark garment.
In reverse order,
[the mantra is] HĀDHARĀVIṢADO NĀNĀGĀNĀṬOPARASĀDRUTA JAMBHAKUṆṬHAKARĀDEVENOJÑĀNADARAMĀRA-SAḤ. (16)
She was indeed bowed down by the weight of the ocean, mines, and the netherworld;
yet she did not find delight in the company of the gods, the gardens, ornaments, or kings.
He sat upon that seat which is the reverse of the flow of tastes, the destroyer of old age and death, and the subduer of the god of love;
he was accompanied by the one who is the sole abode of the new [bliss], having abandoned all sin through the other shore.
He, the giver of cow-wealth and the glory of his lineage, divided that [land] among the villages;
those who subsisted on meat and wine were destroyed within the solar dynasty.
With harsh and unpleasant words and tumultuous cries, they reviled Keśava,
who was the source of all prosperity and the protector of the virtuous.
He was born from a cow, a bull, a goat, a sheep, a ram, a donkey, and a dog;
he was a sudden destroyer of enemies, a bearer of the burden of battle, and one who was free from agitation. 19.
O you who bring about the destruction of enemies, who are free from old age, who bring light to the world, and who perform deeds that defy the impossible;
O bestower of glory upon those who travel through the sky, shine forth once more, O you who are joined with the earth and the gods! 19.
This Lord of Laṅkā, whose intellect is devoid of essence, is one who has destroyed the accumulation of sins;
he is the abandoner of worldly existence, the destroyer of the stream of non-detachment, and the slayer of the demon of ego-grasping.
The terrible, reverse-sequence sound "hā hā paurāte ravir ājirāḥ" was uttered;
and indeed, the one who was firm in the essence of peace fell into the realm of sorrow over what ought to be abandoned.
He was equal in speech to the son of Taṭakī and Lava, possessed a voice that captivated and carried away the heart,
had Sītā as his companion in laughter, and was unassailable on earth by those who were not his kin.
She who possesses a laugh like that of Indra (Ajaya), who was not conquered by the Lord (Vibhu) when he was deprived of Madana;
she who removes the mountain (Giri) along with its waters (Sasara); she who is the destroyer of sin (Hānode); she who is the abode of the gods (Devālaya); she who is the beloved of Keṭa (Keṭatā). 21.
Having crushed the burden [of the enemy] with his own power, and having destroyed the deceitful Rāvaṇa, the forest-guardian Cārudhi took away Vaidehī, who was honored by him. 22.
By means of a verse that was reversed,
which contained the unity of the syllables *tā*, *hṛtāhi*, *mahīdevyaikya*,
*alopa*, and *anavadhīru*, he destroyed the hopes of those of wicked intellect who were devoid of the light of Kumāra. 22.
Hārita, Udabha, Rāma, Viyoga, Gha, Vāyuja, Taṃru, Māmahita, Upeta, Āmoda, Sāra, Jña, and Rāmaya. (23)
In reverse order, from the King of Yamas (Sa) to the end of the Rāsa (Ra), excluding the Himamāruta (Ya);
from the Joy (Ja) to the Youth (Va), and from the Mountain (Ga) to the end of the Vimāra (Ma). || 23 ||
He whose splendor was like that of the sun, who was born from the womb of Ambā, who brought joy to the world,
who destroyed the pride of the gods, who was as beautiful as a lotus, and who had made Indra his servant.
The splendor of the moon-like bodies of those who were delighted by the state of Hara shattered the essence of the agitation caused by the enemy of the twenty winds (the wind-god) acting in reverse.
In that city, which was most auspicious with its noble women whose gait was like that of swans and who possessed the strength of Aruṇa,
Rāma, the destroyer of the pride of the demon Rāvaṇa, went forth to slay the enemy of Ramā (Rāvaṇa).
In reverse order,
it is that which causes the destruction of the enemies of Lakṣmī, which is a field of battle for the hosts of demons,
and which endures the pain caused by the web of arrows produced from its own radiant bow.
The protector of the gods, who surpasses the ocean in luster and subdues the hosts of gods and asuras,
approached that elephant born of the Wind-god and stood before it.
The reverse order of the world,
having attained the state of being devoid of sin through the grace of the Lord,
was filled with joy; yet, due to the intense passion of the beautiful woman, it reached a state of extreme sorrow.
For he was indeed the protector of the heroic monkey army,
having crossed the ocean by means of a bridge that had never been built before.
From the practice of contrary conduct,
from lack of compassion, and from the slaughter of cows,
[the world] shines forth here as if it were the night of the end of the aeon, devoid of the sun and stars.
Indeed, that destroyer of the demon Asura, the beloved of Rāmā (Lakṣmī), who removes the distress of the beautiful Bhūtanuja (Prahlāda), was honored by Hārisāhasalanka. || 28 ||
The reverse [mantra] is:
*vilomaṃ hārtidāyadharāmāramorājonutabhūrucā sahitohimadībhesunākelaṃsahasārihā*. (28)
Indeed, he did not resort to that which was like a coconut, a beautiful form, a house, wine,
a well, the enemy of Rāvaṇa (Rāma), the earth, water, or light.
A certain excellent woman, whose face was radiant with a playful luster like that of a beautiful lotus, looked at him with eyes full of intense passion, as he approached her in reverse order.
She is the cow that bears the burden of the vast sky, which is like a lake of excellent lotuses.
Śrī Rāma, possessing the majesty of a great king, conquered his own body.
Born in the region of Satya, the abode of the glorious Meru,
which is free from the dust of passion; she is fair-complexioned, a destroyer of sins, and her speech is the essence of the highest truth.
Thus ends the *Śrī Rāghavayādavīya* composed by the venerable Veṅkaṭādhvarin.
